name: UnLock Math
line: UnLock Math teaches by video lesson, in course order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs UnLock Math: UnLock Math teaches by video lesson, in course order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: UnLock Math teaches in lessons: a short video, then practice and review, one lesson after another in a course the family chooses [2][3][6]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. UnLock Math offers readiness tests to download, from Pre-Algebra to Pre-Calculus, and the family chooses a course [2][6]. Lessons then run in course order, with a pacing guide [2][6]. Its FAQ mentions an adaptive assessment system and does not say what adapts or how [2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In UnLock Math the unit is the lesson. A five-question Warm-Up comes first, then a short video teaches the new idea, then ten practice questions rising in difficulty, then Stay Sharp review [3]. A wrong answer brings a step-by-step solution [2][3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [9].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. When each skill returns is set by that learner's own answers. In UnLock Math, review is part of every lesson: the Warm-Up brings back five questions from earlier lessons, and Stay Sharp draws ten questions from the previous ten lessons [3]. As its page describes it, review is set by lesson position, not by time [3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [8].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In UnLock Math a learner can take new sets of practice questions without limit [3], and the course moves on in its own order, with a pacing guide [2][6]. Its FAQ says students are not pushed ahead until ideas click, and we found no published rule for when that point is reached [2].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, on one map from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. In UnLock Math the family chooses a course, and lessons follow that course's order [2][6]. Foundations covers grades 2 to 6 in one course, and then come Pre-Algebra through Pre-Calculus [4][5].

rows.range: Foundations covers grades 2 to 6 in one course. Then Pre-Algebra through Pre-Calculus, plus Integrated Math I to III [4][5].
rows.start: Readiness tests to download, from Pre-Algebra to Pre-Calculus. The family chooses the course [2][6].
rows.teaching: Short video lessons taught by Alesia Blackwood, printable notes, live chat with her team (not for California charter students), and a step-by-step solution after a wrong answer [2][3].
rows.next: The next lesson in course order, with a pacing guide [6].
rows.mastery: Graded quizzes, assignments and tests. The FAQ says students are not pushed ahead until ideas click [2].
rows.review: In every lesson: a five-question Warm-Up from earlier lessons, and Stay Sharp, ten questions from the previous ten lessons [3].
rows.print: Printable notes for each lesson and a printable textbook for each course, the same for every student [3].
rows.adult: Picks the course, follows the pacing guide and checks the Gradebook. Grading is automatic [2][6].
rows.reports: A student Report Card and a parent Gradebook of graded quizzes, assignments and tests [2].

theirs: UnLock Math is an online math curriculum for homeschool families. Alesia Blackwood teaches the video lessons on camera [1][3]. The courses run from Foundations, which covers grades 2 to 6 in one course, through Pre-Algebra, Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra 2 and Pre-Calculus, plus Integrated Math I to III [1][4][5]. Its maker describes the method as a hybrid of mastery and spiral teaching [1][3].

Every lesson follows the same pattern. A five-question Warm-Up brings back earlier lessons. A short video teaches the new idea. Ten practice questions follow, one at a time and rising in difficulty, with new sets available without limit. Stay Sharp then reviews the previous ten lessons, and optional Challenge Yourself problems reach further [3]. Quizzes, assignments and tests are graded automatically into a parent Gradebook, and each course comes with a pacing guide [2][6].
credit: A teacher on video for every lesson, and live chat with her team for help, except for California charter students [1][3].
Review in every lesson. The Warm-Up and Stay Sharp bring earlier lessons back each day [3].
A step-by-step solution after a wrong answer [2][3].

theirs: We found no study of UnLock Math's effect on math achievement on its site. The home page links no research page, and its awards page cites no studies [1][7]. It describes its method as a hybrid of mastery and spiral teaching and cites no study of it [1][3].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [9]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks, and the trial meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [8]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child learns best from a teacher on video, with live chat for help.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to come back at growing intervals, set by your child's own answers.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.
You print, and want workbooks made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from UnLock Math?
questions.answer: UnLock Math teaches through a video lesson and its practice, one lesson after another in course order [3][6]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does UnLock Math work?
questions.answer: We found no study of its effect on math achievement on its site [1][7].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
